notes.meaning: Jeremiah was still locked up in the courtyard of the guard, in the king's palace in Jerusalem. God gave him a second message, which builds on the promise of hope in chapter 32. Prison walls could not keep God away. The prophet was bound, but God's word was not.

God introduces himself as the one who plans something, shapes it, and then makes it stand firm. Some take "it" to mean Jerusalem, which God built and will keep. Others take it to mean the plan God is about to carry out. Either way, his name, the LORD, tells us he has the power to keep his word.

God invites his people to call on him, and he promises to answer. He will show "great and unsearchable" things, beyond what people can work out for themselves. Here that means the return of his people, which seemed impossible. God's promises are not meant to replace prayer but to stir it up. The words came to Jeremiah, but they encourage all God's people to pray.

Houses in Jerusalem, even royal palaces, had been torn down during the siege. The siege ramps were mounds of earth the enemy built against the walls. The men of Judah went out to fight the Chaldeans (the Babylonians), but they only filled the houses with their own dead. God says this is his judgment. He has turned his face away from the city because of its wickedness.

"Nevertheless" marks the turn from judgment to hope. God will bind up the city's wounds like a doctor and heal its people. "Peace" stands for every good thing. "Truth" points to God's faithfulness and a lasting security. Matthew Henry sees here a glimpse of the gospel, where grace and truth come through Jesus.

God promises to bring back both Judah and Israel, the whole people, and to rebuild them as they were at the start. The mention of Israel, the northern tribes, points to something bigger than the return from Babylon. Calvin says the promise reaches all the way to the coming of Christ.

God will wash his people clean and forgive every sin, even open rebellion. The word "cleanse" recalls the washings in the old law that made people fit to come near God again. Matthew Henry says cleansing takes away the dirt of sin, and pardon takes away its guilt. The piling up of words shows how great God's grace is. No sin is too big for his mercy, and there is no true joy without forgiveness.

The rebuilt city will bring God joy, praise and honour among all nations as they hear of his goodness. Some say the nations will tremble because they fear to harm a people God so plainly loves. Others, like Calvin, say the nations will come to fear and worship God with awe and joy. Calvin sees in this a picture of the gospel spreading to the world.

The land people called an empty wasteland will be full of happy sounds again. Weddings will return, the very joy that judgment had silenced. People will bring thank offerings to the temple and sing, "Give thanks to the LORD... his loving devotion endures forever." These are the words of Psalm 136. The returning exiles really sang them when the new temple's foundation was laid (Ezra 3:11). Calvin notes that godly joy always turns into thanks to God, together with others.

The empty land will again have pastures where shepherds rest their flocks. Shepherds can only do this when there is peace and no enemy raids. So this is a picture of safety and plenty under God's care.

The list of regions means the whole land of Judah will be lived in again. Shepherds counted their sheep one by one as they passed under their hand. This shows a shepherd's care that not one is lost. Calvin adds that such calm counting only happens in a time of real peace.

"The days are coming": God will surely keep the good promise he made to all his people. For a while his promises may seem asleep, but he will raise them up. Faith means waiting patiently for God's time, trusting his word even when we cannot yet see it fulfilled.

God will make a righteous Branch grow from David's family tree. This repeats the promise of 23:5. The Branch is the Messiah, Christ, the promised king from David's line. Many of David's sons had been wicked kings, but this King will rule with perfect justice. Calvin says Christ rules his people not only by laws but by his Spirit.

Judah will be saved and Jerusalem will live in safety. The city will be called "The LORD Our Righteousness." Righteousness means being right with God. In 23:6 this name belongs to the King himself. Here the city, a picture of the church, shares it, because all her righteousness comes from Christ, not from herself (1 Corinthians 1:30).

God promises that David will never lack a man on Israel's throne. After the exile no king of David's line sat on a throne, so the promise looks forward to Christ, David's son. His kingdom never ends (Luke 1:32-33). There could be a break, but never a final end.

The priests from the tribe of Levi will never lack a man to offer sacrifices before God. The old priesthood later failed and ended. So the traditional reading sees this fulfilled in Christ, the true and lasting priest. It is also fulfilled in his people, who offer spiritual sacrifices of prayer, praise and their own lives.

differ.view: The old priesthood is ended and replaced by Christ. Since the New Testament never calls ministers priests, the verse fits all believers as priests, not pastors.
This promises a gospel ministry that will last in the church to the end of the world, offering pure spiritual worship wherever a church is formed.
This chiefly means the church's spiritual sacrifice of thanksgiving, with Christ as the everlasting priest and sacrifice the old offerings pictured.
The verse should be taken more literally, as pointing to a lasting line of David served by Levitical priests, and it applies to Israel as well as the church.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think verses 14-26 were added later, because they are missing from the ancient Greek translation and the promise of many priests seems to clash with 31:34. Other scholars defend them as Jeremiah's own words.

notes.meaning: God gives Jeremiah another message. A covenant is a binding promise. Just as no one can stop day and night from coming in their time, no one can break God's covenant with David and with the priests. God set the order of day and night after the flood (Genesis 8:22). Matthew Henry says Christ's kingdom may have dark seasons like night, but it will always shine again. Calvin hears a gentle rebuke here for doubting God's faithfulness.

God will multiply David's descendants and the priests until they are as countless as the stars and the sand. This echoes his promise to Abraham. It is focused on the king and the priests because the good of the whole people rested on them. The traditional reading sees it fulfilled in the countless followers of Christ, the true Son of David, and in faithful gospel ministers.

People were saying God had rejected the two families he chose, most likely Judah and Israel. Many think the speakers were unbelieving people of Judah who had given up hope. The Geneva Notes think they were the Babylonians and other unbelievers. Either way, they looked down on God's people as no longer a nation. Yet God still calls them "My people," which shows he has not thrown them away.

God answers with a firm oath. As surely as he set day and night and the laws of heaven and earth, he will not reject Jacob's descendants or David's line. He will bring them back and have compassion on them. Their rescue rests on his mercy alone. Matthew Henry sees this fulfilled in Christ, David's Son, ruling over his people, the "Israel of God" (Galatians 6:16).

differ.view: God means the physical descendants of Israel, not only believers in general. The new covenant reaches the whole world but does not set the nation of Israel aside.
